name: Battle of Hattin
info: On 4 July 1187 the army of the Crusader states, under King Guy of Jerusalem, was surrounded and broken near Tiberias by Saladin's forces, which then took Jerusalem and most Crusader-held towns and prompted the Third Crusade.

facts.date: 4 July 1187, after a march that began on 3 July
facts.place: Near Tiberias and the village of Hittin, beside the double hill known as the Horns of Hattin, in present-day Israel
facts.sides: The Crusader states of the Levant under King Guy of Lusignan, with about 18,000 to 20,000 men including 1,200 knights from Jerusalem and Tripoli and 50 from Antioch; the forces of the Ayyubid Sultanate of Egypt under Sultan Saladin, around 40,000 men including about 12,000 regular cavalry
facts.outcome: Most of the Crusader forces were captured or killed. Saladin then took fifty-two towns and fortifications, and Jerusalem surrendered to him on 2 October 1187.

t: The Crusader army left a well-watered position at La Saphorie against the advice of Raymond III of Tripoli and the Hospitallers, and marched in July heat to a dry plateau where it was surrounded.
Saladin ordered the execution of about 200 Templar and Hospitaller knights and of captured Turcopoles, spared the other captive barons, and had Raynald of Châtillon killed for breaking a truce.
With the field army gone and the castles thinly held, the Crusader kingdom fell quickly, and the defeat led to the Third Crusade.
dyk: Saladin's son al-Afdal, then 17, watched the battle beside his father. He later described how Saladin told him they had not beaten the Franks until Guy's tent fell, and when it fell Saladin dismounted, prostrated himself and wept for joy.
ev: Guy of Lusignan becomes king of Jerusalem in right of his wife Sibylla, over the opposition of Raymond III of Tripoli's faction
Raynald of Châtillon raids a Muslim Hajj caravan during the truce, and in May the Templars are heavily defeated at Cresson
Saladin crosses the Jordan on 30 June and besieges Tiberias on 2 July, where Raymond's wife Eschiva of Bures holds the citadel
On 3 July Guy leaves La Saphorie and marches east, and the army camps without water on the plateau near Meskenah
On 4 July the Crusader army is surrounded and broken, and Guy's tent falls
Saladin has Raynald killed and orders the execution of the captured Templar and Hospitaller knights
Tiberias surrenders on 5 July, and Jerusalem surrenders to Saladin on 2 October
The Third Crusade begins, two years after the battle

sections.background:
Guy of Lusignan became king of Jerusalem in 1186, in right of his wife Sibylla, after the death of her son Baldwin V. The kingdom was divided between a court faction around Guy, made up of Sibylla and relative newcomers such as Raynald of Châtillon, Gerard of Ridefort and the Knights Templar, and a nobles' faction led by Raymond III of Tripoli, who had been regent for the child-king Baldwin V and had opposed Guy's succession. Open warfare was prevented only when Humphrey IV of Toron swore allegiance to Guy.

Saladin had become vizier of Egypt in 1169, took Damascus in 1174 and Aleppo in 1183, and so controlled the southern and eastern flanks of the crusader states. He united his subjects under Sunni Islam, convincing them that he would wage holy war to push the Christian Franks from Jerusalem, although he often made strategic truces with the Franks when problems elsewhere in the Muslim world required it, as he did in 1185.

In 1187 Raynald raided a Muslim Hajj caravan while the truce was in place. Saladin swore to kill him and sent his son al-Afdal and the emir Gökböri to raid the lands around Acre. In May Gerard de Ridefort and the Templars engaged Gökböri at the Battle of Cresson and were heavily defeated, losing around 150 knights and 300 foot soldiers, who had made up a great part of the military of Jerusalem.
sections.forces:
In late May Saladin assembled on the Golan Heights the largest army he had ever commanded, around 40,000 men including about 12,000 regular cavalry, and he crossed the River Jordan on 30 June. The Druze community of Sarahmul, led by Jamal ad-Din Hajji, unexpectedly allied with him. The army stood as a centre under Saladin himself and two wings, the left under Gökböri and the right under Saladin's nephew al-Muzaffar Umar (Taki ad-Din).

The Crusader army gathered at La Saphorie, a well-watered position with a small castle. It numbered around 18,000 to 20,000 men, including 1,200 knights from Jerusalem and Tripoli and 50 from Antioch. The levy was extended, on an occasion of extreme threat, to every able-bodied man in the kingdom. According to some European sources there were also lighter cavalry, perhaps 10,000 foot soldiers, crossbowmen from the Italian merchant fleet and many mercenaries, among them local Turcopoles, hired with money donated by Henry II of England. The Bishop of Acre carried the relic of the True Cross as the army's standard. To field this force the Crusaders had reduced the garrisons of their castles.

Raymond, reconciled with Guy, argued that the army should stay at La Saphorie, that Saladin could not hold Tiberias because his troops would not stay so long from their families, and that he was willing to give up Tiberias for the safety of the kingdom. The Hospitallers also advised against provoking Saladin. Gerard de Ridefort urged an advance, and Gerard and Raynald accused Raymond of cowardice.
sections.course:
On 2 July Saladin led an assault on Raymond's fortress of Tiberias while the main Muslim army stayed at Kafr Sabt. A tower was mined and collapsed and his troops stormed the breach, but Raymond's wife Eschiva of Bures held out in the citadel. Saladin had meant to draw Guy away from La Saphorie, and on 3 July the Frankish army set out, harassed constantly by Muslim archers. The Springs of Turan could not supply it with water. At midday Raymond judged that Tiberias could not be reached by nightfall, and he and Guy turned towards the springs of Kafr Hattin, about 6 miles (9.7 km) away. The Muslims placed themselves between the Franks and the water, and the Franks camped on the arid plateau near Meskenah, so closely surrounded that, in one description, "a cat could not have escaped". During the night the Muslims prayed, sang and beat drums, and set fire to the dry grass.

On the morning of 4 July the crusaders were blinded by smoke and came under fire from Gökböri's mounted archers, resupplied overnight with 400 loads of arrows. Raymond launched two charges towards the water of Lake Tiberias, and after the second he reached the lake and made his way to Tyre. Most of the Christian infantry fled onto the Horns of Hattin and took no further part. Many of Guy's soldiers, overwhelmed by thirst and wounds, were killed where they stood or taken prisoner. The knights and mounted serjeants fought on, but after three charges on Saladin's position they were surrounded and broken up. At the end Guy's tent fell.
sections.aftermath:
The prisoners included Guy, his brother Amalric II, Raynald of Châtillon, William V of Montferrat, Gerard de Ridefort and Humphrey IV of Toron. Saladin offered Guy water, which in Muslim culture was a sign that a prisoner would be spared, though Guy did not know it. Guy passed the cup to Raynald, and Saladin struck it from his hands and charged Raynald with breaking the truce. Baha al-Din and some other reports say Saladin killed Raynald himself with one stroke of the sword; others record that he struck him as a signal to his bodyguards to behead him. Saladin told Guy that "kings do not kill kings". Guy was taken to Damascus and released in 1188, and the other noble captives were eventually ransomed.

All 200 captured Templar and Hospitaller knights were beheaded on Saladin's orders, except the Grand Master of the Temple. Captured Turcopoles were also executed, because Saladin believed them to be converts from Islam, which the law of the Ayyubid state punished with death. The rest of the captured knights and soldiers were sold into slavery. The True Cross was supposedly sent to Damascus fixed upside down on a lance. On 5 July Countess Eschiva surrendered the citadel of Tiberias and was allowed to leave for Tripoli with her family and possessions. Only some 200 knights escaped the battle, and fifty-two towns and fortifications fell to Saladin's forces.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from Muslim and Latin writers. Ali ibn al-Athir describes the Franks as despondent and tormented by thirst and quotes the eyewitness account of Saladin's 17-year-old son al-Afdal. Baha al-Din gives one version of Raynald's death, and Imad ed-Din, Saladin's secretary, describes the execution of the knights. Ernoul's chronicle is the source for the effect of the news on the Pope, and the historians Jonathan Phillips and Norman Housley give their views.

Several points are uncertain. The records of the Crusader council on the night of 2 July are biased by personal feuds among the Franks, so what Raymond, Gerard and Raynald said is known only in outline. The Franks rumoured, and Ibn al-Athir echoed, that Raymond had agreed with Saladin to be made king of Jerusalem in return for peace; it is unclear whether that was true. Housley suggests that Guy took Gerard's advice partly because poisoned political relations led both men to see Raymond's advice as aimed at their ruin, and partly because Guy had spent Henry II's donations on calling the army. The Crusader numbers come in part from European sources, and the figure for the foot soldiers is one given by "some" of them. Saint Nicasius, a Hospitaller later venerated as a Roman Catholic martyr, is said to have been among those executed.
sections.legacy:
The defeat removed the Crusaders' capability to wage war, and Muslims once again became the pre-eminent military power in the Holy Land, recapturing Jerusalem and most other Crusader-held cities and castles. Jerusalem, defended by Queen Sibylla, the Latin Patriarch Heraclius and Balian, surrendered after Balian negotiated its surrender, and Tyre held out because Conrad of Montferrat arrived and Saladin's siege was repulsed with heavy losses.

In the West, according to the chronicler Ernoul, the news brought by Joscius, Archbishop of Tyre, caused Pope Urban III to die of shock. His successor Gregory VIII issued the bull Audita tremendi calling for a new crusade within days of his election, and England and France enacted the Saladin tithe to raise funds. The Third Crusade did not get under way until 1189; it was a very successful military operation through which many Christian holdings were restored. Christian control in the Holy Land nevertheless remained vulnerable for decades, until the Battle of La Forbie in 1244, 57 years after Hattin, which marked the final collapse of Crusader military power in Outremer. The battle is also known as the Battle of the Horns of Hattin, after the shape of the extinct volcano beside the field.

summary: On 4 July 1187 Saladin's army surrounded and broke the army of the Crusader states near Tiberias after it had marched from a well-watered camp into dry country. Most of the Crusaders were killed or captured, and Jerusalem fell on 2 October, leading to the Third Crusade.
notes: The article says Raynald was brought to Saladin's tent with Guy; I attributed the sword-stroke versions as the article does (Baha al-Din 'some reports').
The article's sentence 'Gerard and Raynald advised Guy to form battle lines and attack, which was done by Guy's brother Amalric' is unclear and I left it out.
The article gives the date of the battle as 4 July, with the march on 3 July; the See also list says '3-4 July 1187'. I used 4 July as the date and noted the march.
The article gives no figures for Saladin's casualties, and no Muslim-side numbers for the wounded; none stated.
Not found in the article: any archaeology of the site, the exact Crusader dead, the number of prisoners sold.
In 'Sources' I said Ibn al-Athir 'quotes' al-Afdal's account as the article does; the article does not say when or for whom any of the writers wrote.
